## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Somadattajātaka* (Ja 410) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Jātaka* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya. According to its commentary, the Buddha delivered the story at Jetavana on account of an elderly monk who wept inconsolably after the death of a novice who had attended on him [Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, king of the gods, who intervened to admonish an ascetic who was weeping excessively over the death of a young elephant calf named Somadatta [Fausböll 1883]. Sakka's discourse on the inevitability of death and the futility of mourning cures the ascetic of his sorrow [Fausböll 1883]. At the conclusion of the tale, the Buddha identifies the elephant calf as the deceased novice, the ascetic as the grieving elder, and Sakka as himself [Fausböll 1883]. This story should not be confused with the homonymous *Somadattajātaka* (Ja 211), which concerns a slow-witted brahmin farmer and his courtier son [Fausböll 1879; Bailey and Mabbett 2003].

 DharmaNexus strongly confirms these connections, recording extensive verse-level reuse (notably segments 6.4–9.4 and 7.1–9.4) across Ja 372, Ja 454, Ja 352, Vv 83, Pv 8, Pv 17, Pv 18, and Pv 25, along with their respective commentaries [DharmaNexus; Fausböll 1883]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages of Ja 410 with the Chinese *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100) [DharmaNexus]. In modern scholarship, verses from this Jātaka are cited among canonical texts associated with protective and transformative recitations [Lewis and Tuladhar 2000].
